criteria.description: Correctly explains the low-probability -> high surprise direction (-log p(x) -> infinity as p(x) -> 0).
Correctly explains the near-certain -> near-zero surprise direction (-log p(x) -> 0 as p(x) -> 1).

commonErrors: Only covering one of the two directions.
Not connecting this to everyday intuition about surprise.

solutions.fullSolution: As p(x) -> 0 (a rare event), -log p(x) -> infinity: an extremely unlikely event is maximally surprising, matching everyday intuition. As p(x) -> 1 (a near-certain event), -log p(x) -> 0: an event you already expected shouldn't surprise you at all. This tracks the everyday notion of surprise directly: rare things surprise us more than expected things. The specific -log(.) form (rather than e.g. 1-p(x)) has the further property of being additive across independent events, which is what makes entropy interpretable as an expected code length.

criteria.description: Correctly splits log(p(x)/q(x)) = log p(x) - log q(x).
Correctly uses linearity of expectation to split the difference.
Correctly identifies each expectation term as -H(p) and -H(p,q) respectively, and combines to get H(p,q)-H(p).

commonErrors: Sign errors when identifying E_p{log p(x)} = -H(p) (easy to drop the negative sign since H is DEFINED with a minus sign already).
Not using linearity of expectation explicitly to justify splitting the expectation of a difference.

solutions.fullSolution:
D(p||q) = E_p{log(p(x)/q(x))} = E_p{log p(x) - log q(x)} (splitting the log of a ratio) = E_p{log p(x)} - E_p{log q(x)} (linearity of expectation).

E_p{log p(x)} = -H(p) by definition (H(p) is defined as E_p{-log p(x)}, so E_p{log p(x)} is its negative). Similarly E_p{log q(x)} = -H(p,q) (H(p,q) is defined as E_p{-log q(x)}).

So D(p||q) = -H(p) - (-H(p,q)) = H(p,q) - H(p).

criteria.description: Correctly applies Jensen's inequality with the convex function -log to the ratio q(x)/p(x).
Correctly computes E_p{q(x)/p(x)} = sum_x q(x) = 1 and concludes D(p||q) >= -log(1) = 0.

commonErrors: Using the concave-Jensen direction instead of the convex-Jensen direction (since -log is convex, the inequality direction flips relative to a concave function).
Not recognizing that E_p{q(x)/p(x)} simplifies to sum_x q(x) = 1 specifically because p(x) cancels in the expectation weighting.

solutions.fullSolution:
D(p||q) = E_p{-log[q(x)/p(x)]}. Since -log(.) is convex, Jensen's inequality (for a convex function psi: E[psi(X)] >= psi(E[X])) gives:
E_p{-log[q(x)/p(x)]} >= -log(E_p{q(x)/p(x)}).

Compute the inner expectation: E_p{q(x)/p(x)} = sum_x p(x) * q(x)/p(x) = sum_x q(x) = 1, since q is a valid probability distribution (sums to 1) and p(x) cancels exactly.

So D(p||q) >= -log(1) = 0. Equality in Jensen's inequality holds only when the random quantity (here q(x)/p(x)) is constant, i.e. when p=q everywhere, matching the source's stated equality condition.
